definition.text: A control rule that switches abruptly between two extreme settings, such as fully on and fully off.

facts.text: Most household thermostats are bang–bang controllers: the heater or compressor is either running or not, depending on whether the temperature is above or below the setpoint.
In optimal control, a bang–bang solution is a control that jumps from one bound to the other and never takes an in-between value.
Such solutions appear when the Hamiltonian is linear in the control, so the maximum principle pushes the control to its upper or lower limit.
Bang–bang controls are sometimes truly optimal, but they are also often used simply because they are simple or convenient.

definition.text: An equation from dynamic programming that splits a decision problem over time into a chain of simpler subproblems, following Bellman's principle of optimality.

facts.text: It writes the value of a decision problem at one moment as today's payoff plus the value of the problem left over after today's choice.
Solving it means finding an unknown function, the value function, which gives the best achievable outcome for each state; the matching best action for each state is the policy function.
The name usually refers to discrete-time problems; in continuous time the matching equation is the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman partial differential equation.
It can be solved by backwards induction, by hand in special cases or numerically, but this may be infeasible with many state variables because of the curse of dimensionality.
Economists call dynamic programming a recursive method, because its economic applications usually give a Bellman equation in the form of a difference equation.
It has been used for optimal growth, resource extraction, public finance, asset pricing and many other economic problems.
The first known economic application is credited to Martin Beckmann and Richard Muth; Robert C. Merton's 1973 asset pricing model is a celebrated later one.

title: State and control variables
article: Bellman equation#Analytical concepts in dynamic programming

definition.text: In a decision problem over time, the state is the information about the current situation needed to choose well, and the control variables are what the decision-maker chooses at each moment.

facts.text: Every optimization problem has an objective, such as minimizing cost or maximizing profit, described by a mathematical objective function.
For someone deciding how much to spend over time, wealth is a state variable and how much to consume now is a control variable.
Choosing the controls now may amount to choosing the next state, though other factors usually affect the next state as well.

definition.text: Bellman's rule that an optimal plan has the property that, whatever the starting point and first decision, the remaining decisions must also be optimal from the situation the first decision creates.

facts.text: It tells dynamic programming how to break a decision problem into smaller subproblems.
In computer science, a problem that can be broken apart this way is said to have optimal substructure.
In dynamic game theory, it is analogous to subgame perfect equilibrium.

definition.text: The mathematical study of how the qualitative behaviour of a family of curves or equations, such as the solutions of differential equations, changes as its parameters change.

facts.text: A bifurcation happens when a small smooth change in a parameter causes a sudden qualitative change in how a dynamical system behaves.
Bifurcations occur both in continuous systems described by differential equations and in discrete systems described by maps.
Henri Poincaré introduced the name in 1885.
In ecology, regime shifts linked to a critical or bifurcation point are also called critical transitions.
Systems nearing a bifurcation point show critical slowing down: they recover more and more slowly from disturbances.
Catastrophe theory, which influenced research on regime shifts, is a branch of bifurcation theory.

definition.text: The two main classes of bifurcation: local ones, seen through changes in the stability of equilibria, and global ones, where larger structures of the system collide.

facts.text: A local bifurcation occurs when a parameter change alters the stability of an equilibrium.
Global bifurcations, such as a cycle colliding with an equilibrium, cannot be found just by checking the stability of equilibria.
Saddle-node and Hopf bifurcations are the only generic local bifurcations that truly need just one parameter to be varied.

definition.text: A branch of mathematics that finds the functions which make a quantity defined over whole functions, called a functional, as large or as small as possible.

facts.text: A functional maps a whole function to a single number, so functionals have been described as functions of functions; they are often written as definite integrals.
A simple example is finding the shortest curve joining two points; with no constraints the answer is a straight line.
Just as a function's maxima and minima lie where its derivative is zero, a functional's extrema are found where its functional derivative is zero, which leads to the Euler–Lagrange equation.
The field began with Isaac Newton's minimal resistance problem, solved in 1685, and his 1697 solution of the brachistochrone problem.
In economics, optimization over time has used the calculus of variations, following Frank P. Ramsey and Harold Hotelling.

definition.text: The equation whose solutions are the candidate functions that maximize or minimize a functional in the calculus of variations.

facts.text: It comes from setting the functional derivative to zero, the counterpart of setting an ordinary derivative to zero to find a function's highest or lowest point.
When the variable does not appear on its own in the integrand, the equation simplifies to the Beltrami identity.

definition.text: Finding the best value of an objective, such as a cost to minimize or a utility to maximize, when the choice variables must obey constraints.

facts.text: Hard constraints must be met; soft constraints may be broken, but each violation is penalized in the objective in proportion to how far it goes.
Consumer theory models a buyer's demand on the hypothesis of constrained optimization.
In a typical consumption model over time, discounted utility is maximized subject to a budget constraint that present-value spending cannot exceed present-value resources.
With only equality constraints, Lagrange multipliers turn the problem into an unconstrained one with one extra variable per constraint.
With inequality constraints, the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions generalize Lagrange multipliers and apply under differentiability and convexity.
If the objective and all constraints are linear, the problem is linear programming; if any are nonlinear, it is nonlinear programming.

definition.text: A way to solve a simple constrained problem by plugging the constraint into the objective, leaving an ordinary problem with fewer variables.

facts.text: Example: to maximize x times y with x + y = 10, substitute y = 10 − x to get 10x − x², whose derivative 10 − 2x is zero at x = 5, so y = 5.

definition.text: Constrained optimization in which the objective or some constraints are nonlinear and some constraints are inequalities.

facts.text: Quadratic programming, with linear constraints and a quadratic objective, is one type of nonlinear programming.
A quadratic program with a convex objective can be solved in polynomial time by the ellipsoid method; otherwise it may be NP-hard.

definition.text: A search method for optimization that keeps the cost of the best solution found so far and abandons any partial solution that cannot beat it.

facts.text: Skipping such partial solutions saves part of the search; its efficiency depends on how well the best possible cost of extending a partial solution is estimated.

definition.text: A function whose graph lies on or below the straight line joining any two of its points, so the graph is cup-shaped; a concave function is cap-shaped.

facts.text: A twice-differentiable function of one variable is convex exactly when its second derivative is never negative.
Linear functions, quadratics like cx² with c not negative, and exponentials like ceˣ with c not negative are convex.
Convexity makes optimization easier: any local minimum of a convex function is also a global minimum, and a strictly convex function on an open set has at most one minimum.
A function f is convex exactly when its negative, −f, is concave.
Jensen's inequality: a convex function of an average is never more than the average of the convex function's values.
In consumer theory, a diminishing marginal rate of substitution along an indifference curve means preferences are convex.
Demand curves are generally considered convex, in line with diminishing marginal utility.

definition.text: A convex function that curves upward at least as fast as a quadratic, a stronger condition than strict convexity.

facts.text: Every strongly convex function is strictly convex, but not the other way round.
A strongly convex function has a unique global minimum.
x² is strongly convex, while eˣ is strictly but not strongly convex, because its second derivative can come arbitrarily close to zero.

definition.text: A measure of how sensitive a function's output is to a small change in its input; for a single variable it is the slope of the tangent line at a point.

facts.text: It is often described as the instantaneous rate of change, and finding it is called differentiation.
The tangent line it defines is the best straight-line approximation of the function near that point.
Formally, it is the limit of the ratio of change in output to change in input as the input change shrinks to zero.
A function must be continuous at a point to have a derivative there; a step jump has none.
Rules for sums, products and compositions let derivatives of complex functions be built from those of simple ones.
Leibniz notation, dy/dx, was introduced by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in 1675.
In economics, short-run marginal cost is the slope, or first derivative, of the variable cost curve.

definition.text: The derivative of a function of several variables with respect to one of them, holding the others fixed.

facts.text: It can be read as the function's rate of change in the direction of that one variable.
Partial derivatives measure change only along the coordinate axes; change in other directions is measured by directional derivatives.
The total derivative gives a complete picture by considering all directions at once.

definition.text: The result of differentiating a function repeatedly: the derivative of the derivative is the second derivative, and so on.

facts.text: The nth derivative is the derivative of the (n−1)th derivative.
The sign of the second derivative tells whether a function is convex: a twice-differentiable function of one variable is convex when it is never negative.

definition.text: A function whose derivative is a given function; it runs differentiation in reverse.

facts.text: Antiderivatives are not unique: adding any constant gives another, because a constant's derivative is zero.
By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the integral of a function over an interval equals the difference of an antiderivative's values at the two ends, giving areas under curves.

definition.text: An equation that links one or more unknown functions to their derivatives, that is, to their rates of change.

facts.text: Such relations are common in scientific models, so differential equations are prominent in engineering, physics, economics and biology.
Only the simplest can be solved by explicit formulas, but many properties of the solutions can be found without solving them exactly.
When no formula exists, solutions can be approximated numerically on computers.
The theory of dynamical systems studies qualitative features of the solutions, such as their average long-run behaviour.
They arose with the invention of calculus by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz; Newton listed three kinds in a 1671 work.
They are used to model almost every physical, technical or biological process, from celestial motion to bridge design to neurons.
Complex adaptive systems may have so many elements that a system of differential equations becomes impractical and stops helping understanding.

definition.text: The main ways differential equations are classified: ordinary or partial, linear or nonlinear, homogeneous or not, and by order.

facts.text: An ordinary differential equation has an unknown function of one variable; a partial differential equation has unknown functions of several variables and their partial derivatives.
Linear differential equations have a well-developed theory, while few nonlinear ones can be solved exactly and they can behave chaotically over long times.
The order is the highest derivative that appears; equations describing nature usually have only first and second derivatives.
The class of an equation helps guide the choice of solution method.

title: Initial conditions
article: Differential equation#Initial conditions and boundary conditions

definition.text: Extra information, such as a system's starting values, needed to pin down which of a differential equation's many solutions applies.

facts.text: The general solution of an nth-order ordinary differential equation contains n undetermined constants.
For a moving particle, the initial conditions are usually its position and velocity at the starting time.

definition.text: An equation in which time or another variable takes only separate values, relating a quantity's value at one point to its values at nearby points.

facts.text: Difference equations, also called recurrence relations, are the discrete-time counterpart of differential equations.
Numerical methods such as the Euler method approximate a differential equation by a matching difference equation.
Economists can model a price adjusting to excess demand either as a difference equation or, in continuous time, as a differential equation.
The Beverton–Holt population model is a discrete-time analogue of Verhulst's continuous-time logistic growth equation.

definition.text: Two alternative ways of modelling variables that change over time: as values in separate periods, or as values at every instant.

facts.text: Discrete time treats a variable as fixed within each period and jumping between periods, like a digital clock jumping from 10:37 to 10:38.
Continuous time lets time range over the real numbers, so there are infinitely many moments between any two points in time.
Economic activity happens continuously but can only be measured in steps, so GDP data come as a series of quarterly values.
Discrete time suits empirical work and time series models, while continuous-time theoretical models are often easier to handle mathematically.
Discrete time uses difference equations; continuous time uses differential equations.
Total discounted utility from a stream of consumption is a sum in discrete time and an integral in continuous time.

definition.text: The principle that any optimization problem can be viewed from two sides, the original (primal) problem or a matching dual problem.

facts.text: If the primal is a minimization problem, the dual is a maximization problem, and vice versa.
Any feasible value of the primal minimization is at least as large as any feasible value of the dual, so each bounds the other.
The usual Lagrangian dual adds the constraints to the objective using non-negative Lagrange multipliers, which become the dual variables.
Each constraint in an optimization problem has a shadow price, or dual variable.
In microeconomics, minimizing the spending needed to reach a level of happiness is the dual of maximizing utility.
John von Neumann conjectured the duality theorem of linear programming, drawing on his game theory; Albert W. Tucker's group published the first rigorous proofs in 1948.

definition.text: The difference between the optimal values of a primal optimization problem and its dual.

facts.text: For minimization problems the gap is never negative.
Strong duality holds when the gap is zero; otherwise it is positive and only weak duality holds.
For convex problems the gap is zero when a constraint qualification such as Slater's condition holds.

definition.text: A method of optimization, and a style of computer algorithm, that solves a complex problem by breaking it recursively into simpler subproblems.

facts.text: Richard Bellman developed it in the 1950s, and it is used in fields such as aerospace engineering and economics.
Decisions that span several points in time often break apart this way, even though some problems cannot.
The relation between the value of the whole problem and the values of its subproblems is called the Bellman equation.
Values are found by working backward from the last period, computing each earlier period's value from the next one.
In computer science it needs two features: optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems; without overlap the approach is called divide and conquer.
It is widely used in bioinformatics, for example in sequence alignment and protein folding.

title: Ramsey's optimal saving problem
article: Dynamic programming#Example from economics: Ramsey's problem of optimal saving

definition.text: A classic economic planning problem of choosing how much to consume now and how much to invest in capital for future consumption.

facts.text: The planner maximizes a social welfare function linking consumption to utility, with future consumption discounted at a constant rate.
Dynamic programming lets the consumer decide one step at a time, choosing only current consumption and saving given current capital.
In the worked example, it is optimal to consume a larger share of wealth with age, using up everything in the last period of life.

definition.text: Growth in which a quantity increases at a rate proportional to its current size, so the bigger it gets, the faster it grows.

facts.text: Something three times bigger is growing three times as fast; a bacterium splitting into 2, then 4, 8, 16 and 32 is the usual illustration.
Exponential growth is not the same as rapid growth: it can be slow at first.
Economic growth is stated in percentages, implying exponential growth, and compound interest at a constant rate grows capital exponentially.
A bacterium that doubles every ten minutes becomes 64 bacteria after one hour.
If the constant of proportionality is negative, the quantity shrinks instead, which is exponential decay.
Over the long run, exponential growth overtakes any linear growth, which is the basis of the Malthusian catastrophe.
Malthus warned that population growing geometrically, doubling every 25 years, would outrun food production growing arithmetically.
Real exponential growth rarely lasts: external limits eventually slow it into logistic growth.

sources.title: An Essay on the Principle of Population

definition.text: Growth that starts out exponential but slows as it approaches an upper limit set by external or environmental factors.

facts.text: Population growth, for instance, may level off at an upper limit because resources run short.
Belgian mathematician Pierre François Verhulst first proposed this growth model in 1845.
It arises when negative feedbacks ignored in the exponential model become significant.
The discrete-time Beverton–Holt population model is the analogue of Verhulst's continuous-time logistic equation.
Pierre François Verhulst devised it between 1838 and 1847 as a model of population growth, adjusting the exponential growth model.
He wrote it after reading Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population, which describes unconstrained exponential growth.
In ecology the model is dP/dt = rP(1 − P/K), where r is the growth rate and K the carrying capacity.
As the population grows, competition for critical resources slows growth until the population stops growing at K.

definition.text: The human tendency to underestimate how quickly compounding processes grow.

facts.text: Studies show people find exponential growth hard to grasp, and the bias can have financial consequences.
In the rice-on-a-chessboard legend, doubling the grains on each square demands over a million grains by the 21st square and more than a trillion by the 41st.
In the water lily riddle, a plant doubling daily covers half the pond on day 29, leaving only one day to save it.

definition.text: Rewriting exponential growth so that the logarithm of the growing quantity rises in a straight line over time.

facts.text: This lets an exponentially growing variable be modelled with a log-linear model.
To estimate a growth rate from data over time, one can run a linear regression of log x on time.

definition.text: A function built to solve an optimal control problem, combining the objective with the equations that describe how the system's state changes.

facts.text: Lev Pontryagin developed it as part of his maximum principle; it was inspired by, but differs from, the Hamiltonian of classical mechanics.
Pontryagin proved that a necessary condition for optimal control is that the control be chosen to optimize the Hamiltonian at each moment.
It works like a Lagrangian in static optimization, except that its multipliers, called costate variables, change over time.
The state and costate equations together form a two-point boundary value problem, with conditions at the start and end times.
It can be seen as a device for generating the first-order necessary conditions of a dynamic optimization problem.
A sufficient condition for a maximum is that the Hamiltonian be concave at the solution.

title: Current value Hamiltonian
article: Hamiltonian (control theory)#Current value and present value Hamiltonian

definition.text: A version of the control Hamiltonian, common in economics, that strips out exponential discounting so that values are measured at the current date.

facts.text: In economic dynamic optimization the objective often depends on time only through exponential discounting of an instantaneous utility, or felicity, function.
Its costate variables are economically the current-valued shadow prices of the capital goods.

definition.text: An end-point condition needed for optimality in a dynamic problem whose final state is left free.

facts.text: With a free terminal value, the costate variable must equal zero at the final time.
In a lifetime consumption problem, a transversality condition says the consumer carries no debt at the end of life.
If the terminal time tends to infinity, a transversality condition on the Hamiltonian applies.

definition.text: Optimization in which some or all of the choice variables must be whole numbers.

facts.text: Usually it means integer linear programming, where the objective and other constraints are linear; if only some variables are integers it is mixed-integer programming.
Integers are used for quantities that cannot be fractional, since it is not possible to build 3.7 cars, and for yes-or-no decisions coded as 0 or 1.
An agricultural example is planning yields for several crops that share land, labour, capital, seeds and fertilizer, maximizing production without exceeding resources.
Integer programming is NP-complete, so many instances are intractable and heuristic methods such as tabu search are used.
Exact methods include cutting planes and variants of branch and bound.
Districting problems, including waste management districting, are solved this way, respecting natural boundaries and contiguity.

definition.text: The linear program obtained by dropping the whole-number requirement from an integer program.

facts.text: Rounding the LP relaxation's solution is the naive approach, but the result may be neither optimal nor even feasible.
If the constraint matrix is totally unimodular, the simplex method's solution is guaranteed to be whole numbers.

definition.text: First-derivative tests that an optimal solution of a nonlinear programming problem must pass, provided certain regularity conditions hold.

facts.text: They extend the method of Lagrange multipliers, which allows only equality constraints, to problems with inequality constraints.
Harold W. Kuhn and Albert W. Tucker published them in 1951; William Karush had stated them in an unpublished 1939 master's thesis.
With no inequality constraints, they reduce to the Lagrange conditions and the KKT multipliers become Lagrange multipliers.
Many optimization algorithms can be read as ways of numerically solving the KKT system of equations and inequalities.
They are also sufficient for an optimum when a maximization's objective is concave, its inequality constraints convex, its equality constraints affine and Slater's condition holds.
Economists use them to get qualitative results, for example that a firm maximizing sales revenue subject to a minimum profit produces where marginal revenue is below marginal cost.
Each multiplier is the rate at which the best achievable value rises as its resource constraint is loosened, an interpretation used in utility maximization.

title: Complementary slackness
article: Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions#Interpretation: KKT conditions as balancing constraint-forces in state space

definition.text: The KKT condition that an inequality constraint which is not binding at the optimum gets a multiplier of zero.

facts.text: It is often written as the product of each multiplier and its constraint being zero.
Picturing the solution as a particle, a constraint can only push back when the particle touches its boundary.

definition.text: A regularity condition that guarantees that the optimum of a constrained problem satisfies the KKT conditions.

facts.text: The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) is the most frequently used.
Slater's condition applies to convex problems: some point must satisfy the inequality constraints strictly.
Weaker qualifications are preferred in practice because they cover more problems.

definition.text: A method for finding the highest or lowest value of a function when the choice variables must satisfy one or more equations exactly.

facts.text: It is named after the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange.
It turns a constrained problem into one where the ordinary derivative test for unconstrained problems can be used, through a new function called the Lagrangian.
At a constrained optimum, the gradient of the objective is a linear combination of the constraints' gradients.
Each multiplier measures how fast the optimized quantity changes as its constraint is relaxed.
In economic models such as general equilibrium, consumers maximize utility and firms maximize profit under budget and production constraints, usually solved with Lagrange multipliers.
In optimal control, the multipliers become costate variables in Pontryagin's maximum principle.
The principle of maximum entropy used in cost–benefit analysis under uncertainty also relies on Lagrange multipliers.

definition.text: A method for finding the best outcome, such as maximum profit or lowest cost, in a model where the goal and all the requirements are linear relationships.

facts.text: It optimizes a linear objective subject to linear equality and inequality constraints, and is a special case of mathematical optimization.
Its feasible region is a convex polytope, the shape cut out by the linear inequalities.
Example: a farmer with limited land, fertilizer and pesticide chooses how many hectares of wheat and barley to plant to maximize revenue.
Leonid Kantorovich and Wassily Leontief independently explored its practical uses in the late 1930s; Kantorovich and T. C. Koopmans shared the 1975 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.
George B. Dantzig developed the general formulation in 1946–1947 for US Air Force planning and invented the simplex method in 1947.
It was heavily used in the early formation of microeconomics and helped inspire key ideas in optimization such as duality and the importance of convexity.
The earliest precursor of William Nordhaus's DICE climate-economy model was a linear programming model of energy supply and demand from 1977.

definition.text: George Dantzig's 1947 method for linear programming, which starts at a corner of the feasible region and walks along its edges to better corners until it reaches the optimum.

facts.text: Dantzig's original example, assigning 70 people to 70 jobs, has more possible arrangements than particles in the observable universe, yet the simplex method solves it in a moment.
Khachiyan's 1979 ellipsoid method was the first worst-case polynomial-time algorithm for linear programming, though simplex remained faster in practice.
Today good simplex and interior-point implementations are thought to be similarly efficient for routine problems.

definition.text: A non-negative extra variable added to a linear program to turn an inequality constraint into an equality.

facts.text: In the farm example, the slack variables stand for the unused land, unused fertilizer and unused pesticide.
Rewriting a problem with slack variables puts it in the augmented form used by the simplex algorithm.

definition.text: A mathematical model of making a sequence of decisions when outcomes are uncertain.

facts.text: It is defined by states, actions, the probabilities of moving between states, and rewards.
The goal is a policy, a rule giving the action for each state, that maximizes the expected discounted sum of rewards.
MDPs arose in operations research in the 1950s and are now used in ecology, economics, healthcare and reinforcement learning.
They are often solved with stochastic dynamic programming, where the Bellman equation gives the recursion for expected rewards.
The curse of dimensionality often makes exact solution infeasible because problem size grows exponentially with the number of state and action variables.
A Markov decision process is a stochastic game with only one player.
Real options can be valued by recasting them as a data-driven Markov decision process solved with deep reinforcement learning.

definition.text: The standard algorithms for finding the best policy in a finite Markov decision process, repeatedly updating a value for each state and a chosen action for each state.

facts.text: Value iteration, also called backward induction (Bellman 1957), starts from a guess of the value function and improves it step by step.
Policy iteration alternates computing values and improving the policy until the policy stops changing, giving a definite stopping point.
Howard invented policy iteration to optimize Sears catalogue mailing.

definition.text: Choosing the best option, judged by some criterion, from a set of available alternatives.

facts.text: Typically it means maximizing or minimizing a function by choosing inputs from an allowed set.
It splits into discrete optimization, where the answer comes from a countable set such as whole numbers, and continuous optimization.
Optimization problems arise in every quantitative field, from engineering to operations research and economics.
An influential definition calls economics the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means with alternative uses.
Consumers are usually assumed to maximize utility and firms to maximize profit; utility maximization and its dual, expenditure minimization, are standard examples.
Since the 1970s economists have modelled decisions over time with control theory.
Fermat and Lagrange found calculus-based formulas for optima, while Newton and Gauss proposed step-by-step methods for moving towards one.
The 'programming' in linear programming comes from the US military's word for training and logistics schedules, not computer programming.

definition.text: The tests a candidate solution must pass: first-order conditions set the derivative to zero, and second-order conditions tell maxima from minima.

facts.text: By one of Fermat's theorems, optima of unconstrained problems lie at stationary points, where the first derivative or gradient is zero.
More generally, optima can also lie where the derivative is undefined or on the boundary of the choice set.
The first derivative test cannot tell a minimum from a maximum; checking the second derivative, or the Hessian matrix, can.
Weierstrass's extreme value theorem says a continuous function on a compact set reaches both a maximum and a minimum.

definition.text: Optimization with more than one goal, where conflicting goals force a trade-off.

facts.text: A design is Pareto optimal if no other design is better on one criterion without being worse on another; the best trade-offs trace out the Pareto frontier.
Choosing among Pareto optimal solutions is left to the decision-maker, because how to weigh the goals is missing information.
Portfolio optimization is an economic example of multi-objective optimization.

definition.text: The branch of control theory that finds how to steer a system that changes over time so that an objective is optimized over a period.

facts.text: The system might be a spacecraft reaching the Moon on minimum fuel, or a national economy where fiscal and monetary policy are used to minimize unemployment.
It extends the calculus of variations and was developed mainly by Lev Pontryagin and Richard Bellman in the 1950s.
The optimal control can be found from Pontryagin's maximum principle, a necessary condition, or by solving the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation, a sufficient condition.
Example: how should a driver press the accelerator on a hilly road to minimize travel time, given limits such as fuel and speed limits?
A classic resource example is a mine owner choosing how fast to extract ore over the period of ownership to maximize profit, when extraction costs rise with speed.
Most optimal control problems are nonlinear with no exact solution, so numerical methods are needed.
Finding the best strategy in a differential game is closely related to optimal control.

definition.text: In optimal control, a variable, sometimes called the shadow price, that gives the marginal value of having a little more or less of the state variable.

facts.text: Its marginal value covers not only the next period's gain but the whole remaining duration of the program.
Solving for the costate first is a common strategy; the optimal control can then usually be found from it.
Costate variables play the role that Lagrange multipliers play in static problems, but change over time.

definition.text: A special case of optimal control with linear dynamics and a quadratic cost, which can be solved in feedback form.

facts.text: Its cost can be read physically as minimizing control energy.
The optimal control is a feedback rule proportional to the state, with the matrix found from the Riccati equation.

definition.text: A picture of a dynamical system's possible paths drawn in the phase plane, with each starting point giving its own curve.

facts.text: It shows typical trajectories with arrows, stable steady states as dots and unstable ones as circles.
It reveals whether an attractor (a stable point or sink), a repeller (an unstable point or source) or a limit cycle is present.
For a system of ordinary differential equations it shows whether the system is unstable, asymptotically stable or neutrally stable.
Its shape, such as a saddle, node or spiral, can be read off the eigenvalues, or the trace and determinant, of the system.

definition.text: A rule in optimal control theory for finding the best way to steer a dynamical system from one state to another, especially when states or controls are constrained.

facts.text: It says an optimal control and its state path must solve the Hamiltonian system, a two-point boundary value problem, and maximize the control Hamiltonian.
Lev Pontryagin and his students formulated it in 1956; its first use was maximizing a rocket's final speed.
Its power is that maximizing the Hamiltonian at each moment is much easier than optimizing over whole functions.
The conditions are necessary, and become sufficient under certain convexity conditions.
Unlike the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation, which must hold over the whole state space, its conditions need only hold along one path, which can make it more efficient to compute.
In differential games, open-loop strategies are found with the maximum principle and closed-loop strategies with dynamic programming.

title: Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation

definition.text: The partial differential equation that plays the role of the Bellman equation in continuous-time optimization problems.

facts.text: Solving it gives a sufficient condition for an optimal control, while Pontryagin's principle gives a necessary one.
It provides a necessary and sufficient condition for an optimum and extends easily to stochastic optimal control problems.
It is used to find optimal policies in continuous-time Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions.

notes: No article of its own crawled; passes test 5 (Bellman equation, Dynamic programming, Optimal control, Pontryagin's maximum principle, Markov decision process).

definition.text: The study of whether the solutions of differential equations and the paths of dynamical systems stay close when their starting conditions are disturbed slightly.

facts.text: It asks whether a nearby path will stay close to a given one forever, and whether it will converge to it.
An equilibrium is stable if starting close keeps a system close, and asymptotically stable if the system also returns to it over time.
A key idea is to analyze behaviour near an equilibrium by linearizing the system, where eigenvalues of a matrix describe how nearby points move.
If all eigenvalues have negative real parts, the point is a stable attracting fixed point that nearby points approach at an exponential rate.
In economics, a price adjusting to excess demand converges to equilibrium only if the derivative of its rate of change with respect to price is negative.
Stability can also be applied to Nash equilibria; Cournot introduced best-response dynamics in studying the stability of equilibrium.

definition.text: An equilibrium is stable if a small push leads only to small, local movement, and unstable if a small push can send the system far away.

facts.text: A pendulum shows stable equilibrium with small oscillations; a ball resting on top of a hill shows unstable equilibrium.
With damping, a stable equilibrium is also asymptotically stable.
For an iterated map, a fixed point is stable if the derivative there is less than 1 in absolute value and unstable if greater.

title: Lyapunov function
article: Stability theory#Lyapunov function for general dynamical systems

definition.text: A function of a system's state whose existence demonstrates that the system is stable.

facts.text: Lyapunov functions are a general way to prove that a dynamical system is stable or asymptotically stable.
It is often useful to picture a Lyapunov function as the energy of the system.
Aleksandr Lyapunov showed in 1892 that systems of ordinary differential equations behave stably given a suitable Lyapunov function.

title: Steady state

definition.text: The condition of a system whose defining variables are not changing over time.

facts.text: In continuous time the rate of change of each property is zero; in discrete time each period-to-period difference is zero.
Many systems pass through a transient, warm-up period before reaching steady state, and often only approach it gradually.
A reservoir in a biogeochemical box model is in steady state when its sources balance its sinks.
In the Solow–Swan growth model, the steady state is reached when gross investment in physical capital equals depreciation.
Exogenous growth models without technological change predict that economies converge to a steady state with zero per-capita growth.
A steady-state economy has a stable population and stable consumption at or below carrying capacity.
An unstable system moves away from its steady state.

title: Computable general equilibrium

definition.text: A class of economic models that use real economic data to estimate how a whole economy might respond to changes in policy, technology or other outside factors.

facts.text: A CGE model is a set of equations plus a detailed database consistent with them, usually assuming cost-minimizing producers and optimizing households.
They estimate how a change in one part of the economy spreads to the rest: a tax on flour might affect bread prices, the CPI, and then wages and employment.
Unlike input–output models, from which they descend, they let prices matter, so a wage rise can change how much labour is used to make bread.
They have been used widely for trade policy and, more recently, to estimate the economic effects of cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
For climate policy they can show gains and losses across groups, such as households with different incomes or in different regions.
Many are comparative static, comparing the economy with and without a policy shock at one future point, without modelling the adjustment path.
They are useful where time-series data are scarce, so developing economies are often analysed with them.
Most are now built in the GAMS or GEMPACK software systems, which lowered costs and made models more transparent and replicable.

title: Model closure

definition.text: In a CGE model, the choice of which variables are set from outside (exogenous) rather than worked out by the model (endogenous).

facts.text: CGE models always have more variables than equations, so some must be fixed outside the model.
Technology, consumer tastes and government instruments such as tax rates are usually exogenous.
Modellers differ: some hold employment and the trade balance fixed, while others let them vary.

contested_note: The choice of closure can be controversial, since modellers disagree on whether employment and the trade balance should be fixed or free.

title: Nested CES structure
article: Computable general equilibrium#Role of separability and nested structures

definition.text: The usual way CGE models represent production and consumption: layered constant elasticity of substitution (CES) functions in which groups of goods or inputs are treated as composites.

facts.text: A firm may first choose among capital, labour, materials and energy, then decide the mix within each; households may split spending across food, housing and transport first.
This multi-stage choice is consistent only if preferences or technologies are separable in the relevant groups.
Separability makes CGE models computationally tractable and lets them be calibrated to reproduce observed base-year data.
